exercises.prompt: What does an esthetic judgment ask about a work?

choices.text: What it does as a selective re-creation
Whether you agree with the philosophy it embodies
Whether the philosophy is true, and nothing about the work
Whether you feel loyal to the artist

feedback.note: An esthetic judgment asks what the work does as a selective re-creation. Agreement with its philosophy is a separate question, and truth alone, with nothing said about the work, never reaches the art. Loyalty to the artist is subjectivism. The esthetic question stays on the re-creation the work actually presents. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: Agreeing with the philosophy a work embodies answers which question?

choices.text: The philosophical question, which is not yet an esthetic judgment
The esthetic question, because agreement is the whole of it
Both questions at once, because they cannot come apart
Neither, because philosophy is irrelevant to every work

feedback.note: Agreement answers whether you accept the ideas. It does not grade the selective re-creation. Treating agreement as the esthetic judgment collapses the two questions. They can come apart in either direction. Philosophy is not irrelevant: it is embodied, and still the question of its truth is not the question of what the work does as art.

exercises.prompt: A reader finds a novel's view of man false, and also finds that the plot embodies that view with strict control. What may the reader conclude?

choices.text: The philosophy can be rejected, and the esthetic question remains open
Disagreement ends the esthetic question, so the work fails as art
Disagreement is forbidden once the plot is clear
Agreement and esthetic success are one verdict under two names

feedback.note: Rejection of the philosophy leaves the esthetic question open, because that question asks what the work does as a re-creation. Disagreement does not prove esthetic failure, and clarity does not forbid philosophical rejection. One verdict under two names collapses the questions. The reader can answer them differently.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to the judgment it belongs to.

pairs.left: What does the work do as a re-creation?
pairs.right: Esthetic judgment
Philosophical judgment

pairs.left: Do I share the artist's metaphysics?
pairs.right: Agreement, not a grade of the art

pairs.left: Is the view embodied by the means?
pairs.right: An esthetic question about the work itself

feedback.note: What the work does, and whether its means embody the view, are esthetic. Whether the philosophy is true, and whether you share it, are not grades of the art. Mixing a row treats loyalty or truth as if it were the re-creation. The rows stay distinct because skill and truth can come apart.

exercises.prompt: Complete the split between the two questions.

parts.text: Esthetic judgment asks what the work
as art, which is not whether you

feedback.note: Does names the esthetic question: what the selective re-creation accomplishes. Agree names the separate philosophical question. Pay substitutes a price, and obey substitutes a command. Neither is a judgment of the work as art. The split stands because a reader can reject the ideas and still judge the re-creation, or accept the ideas and still find the work failing.

exercises.prompt: Which remark collapses the two questions?

choices.text: If the metaphysics is false, the work is esthetically worthless
I reject the metaphysics, and I can still judge the re-creation
Agreement would not by itself make a muddled work succeed
The two questions can be answered in opposite ways

feedback.note: False metaphysics does not settle esthetic worth, because the esthetic question is what the work does as a selective re-creation. The other remarks keep the questions apart: rejection leaves the art open, agreement does not rescue a muddle, and the answers can oppose each other. The collapse treats philosophical error as if it were an esthetic method.

exercises.prompt: A committee praises a clumsy pageant because it says the right thing about man's efficacy. Which question did they answer?

choices.text: They agreed with a philosophy and skipped what the work does as art
They gave an esthetic judgment and skipped nothing
They judged the means and ignored a slogan
They separated the questions and answered both

feedback.note: Praise for saying the right thing, while the pageant is clumsy, is philosophical agreement used as if it were esthetic judgment. They did not judge the re-creation, did not weigh the means, and did not answer both questions. Efficacy may be a true appraisal and still not be shown by interchangeable scenes and a speech. The skip is the esthetic question.

exercises.prompt: Build the split in the order that keeps its meaning.

tokens.text: , and agreement is a separate question

feedback.note: Esthetic judgment asks what the work does as a selective re-creation, and agreement is a separate question. Making it the same as agreement, or turning it into a loyalty test, collapses the split. The substitutes change the claim because one can welcome or oppose the philosophy and still have the esthetic question left to answer on the work itself.

exercises.prompt: Judging what the work does means judging which thing?

choices.text: The selective re-creation it actually presents
A slogan printed beside it
The author's biography
A lecture that could replace the work

feedback.note: The esthetic object is the selective re-creation presented in the work. A slogan beside it, a biography, and a lecture that could replace the work are all outside that re-creation. Art's basic purpose is to show, not to teach, so a lecture standing in for the work does not do what the judgment asks. The judgment stays on what is shown.

exercises.prompt: The preface says man can choose, but the story is a string of accidents with no chosen climax. What should the esthetic judgment weigh?

choices.text: The story actually presented, which does not show volition
The preface, because a slogan is the work
The preface, because the purpose of art is to teach the sentence
The author's diary, because purpose lives only there

feedback.note: The story is a record of accidents, so it does not show volition, whatever the preface claims. A slogan is not the work, and teaching the sentence is not the basic purpose. The diary is not the re-creation either. The judgment weighs what the work shows. Here the concretes contradict the pasted sentence.

exercises.prompt: A film ends with a card ordering the audience to sacrifice, and the scenes never embody a view of man. What is the failure?

choices.text: A propaganda command stands in for the re-creation the work was to show
The film fails because it uses pictures rather than a lecture
The film succeeds because teaching a command is the purpose of art
The film succeeds because a card is a metaphysical value-judgment by itself

feedback.note: The card is a propaganda order, and the scenes do not show a view of man and existence. Pictures are not the failure; the failure is that they do not carry the meaning. Teaching a command is not the purpose. A card is not a metaphysical value-judgment embodied in the work. The purpose is to show, and this film does not.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role it can play in an esthetic judgment.

pairs.right: What the judgment actually weighs
The basic purpose: a concretized image of man and his place
What the basic purpose is not
A sentence that does not do the work's job

feedback.note: The judgment weighs the re-creation, whose purpose is to show a concretized image of man's nature and place, not to teach. A slogan beside the work can state a truth and still not be what the work does. Treating the slogan or the lecture as the art confuses a philosophical sentence with the selective re-creation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the basic purpose that an esthetic judgment has to respect.

feedback.note: Show names the purpose: a concretized image of man's nature and his place in the universe. Teach is what the purpose is not. Order would make the work a propaganda command, and record would make it an unselective news photograph. The judgment looks for what is shown in the work, not for a lesson or a dump standing in its place. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the basic purpose of art?
exercises.quote: The basic purpose of art is not to teach, but to show—to hold up to man a concretized image of his nature and his place in the universe.

choices.text: The purpose is to show a concretized image of man's nature and place, not to teach
The purpose is to teach, and showing is a lesser substitute
The purpose is to issue a command, as a propaganda poster does
The purpose is to record an event, as a news photograph does

feedback.quote: The basic purpose of art is not to teach, but to show—to hold up to man a concretized image of his nature and his place in the universe.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Psycho-Epistemology of Art," The Romantic Manifesto, 21
feedback.note: The passage sets showing above teaching, and the thing shown is a concretized image of man's nature and place. Reversing show and teach contradicts the sentence. A propaganda command and a news record are the morality-play and unselective-record rivals. They fail because the purpose is to show the image, not to order or to inventory.

exercises.prompt: Which work is doing what the purpose of art names?

choices.text: A play that shows an intelligible image of a man facing a choice he could refuse
A tract that teaches the same sentence and calls the binding a work of art
A photograph that tries to catch every bystander at equal weight
A poster whose only content is the order to obey the state

feedback.note: The play shows a concretized image of a chooser, which is the purpose. The tract teaches and merely wears the binding of art. The photograph is an unselective record. The poster is a statist command, a propaganda substitute for showing. Only the play does what an esthetic judgment should find the work doing. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule of judgment in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Judge what the work shows as a selective re-creation, not a slogan beside it. The lecture in the preface and a command to agree are the teaching substitutes. Either one changes the rule, because the basic purpose is to show a concretized image of man and his place. A true sentence outside the work has not yet been shown.

exercises.prompt: Which pair can come apart in an esthetic judgment?

choices.text: Artistic skill and the truth of the philosophy the work embodies
An intelligible subject and the requirement of intelligibility
Inclusion and the act of selection
A plot and the events that constitute that plot

feedback.note: Skill and truth can come apart in either direction: a false view can be brilliantly embodied, and a true view can be clumsily embodied. Intelligibility is the requirement a subject must meet, not a rival of it. Inclusion is part of selection. A plot is constituted by its events. Only skill and philosophical truth are independent verdicts. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: A novel is masterfully plotted, and it presents man as a determined puppet. You hold that this view is false. What follows?

choices.text: The skill can be recognized, and the philosophy can still be rejected
The skill is a vote that the philosophy is true
The false philosophy proves that the skill is unreal
Rejection of the philosophy forbids noticing the plot's control

feedback.note: Masterful plotting is skill at the re-creation, and it does not vote the puppet view true. Nor does the false view erase the skill. Forbidding yourself to notice the control collapses truth into skill in the other direction. The two verdicts come apart: recognize what the work does, and reject the philosophy on its own grounds.

exercises.prompt: A novel advocates a view you hold, that man can choose, but the events are accidental and the point is only in a speech. What follows?

choices.text: Agreement does not supply the skill, and the work can fail as a re-creation
Agreement makes the work esthetically successful
The true view turns the accidents into a plot
A speech is skill, because the philosophy is true

feedback.note: A true philosophy does not repair accidental events or turn a speech into a plot. Agreement is not esthetic success. Skill would be the purposeful re-creation, which is missing. The case is the other direction of the split: truth without the artistic control that would show it. The speech teaches; it does not do the work.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the pair of verdicts it permits.

pairs.left: Skilled, and the view is false
pairs.right: Recognize the skill and reject the philosophy

pairs.left: Unskilled, and the view is true
pairs.right: Keep the agreement and admit the esthetic failure

pairs.left: Skilled, and the view is true
pairs.right: Both verdicts can be affirmative together

pairs.left: Truth used as the only esthetic test
pairs.right: The collapse of skill into a loyalty test

feedback.note: The first three cases show that skill and truth can stand together or come apart either way. The fourth is the error of using agreement as the esthetic test. None of the successful splits makes skill a proof of the philosophy or truth a substitute for the re-creation. The method is to answer both questions, not to let one swallow the other. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: Complete the independence of the two verdicts.

parts.text: is not evidence that the philosophy is

feedback.note: Skill is the control of the re-creation, and true is the separate philosophical verdict it does not prove. Mood would make the test emotional, and price would make it commercial. Neither is evidence of a metaphysics. The sentence blocks one direction of the collapse; the other direction, a true view proving skill, is equally a mistake.

exercises.prompt: Which error treats a crowd's response as proof of the philosophy?

choices.text: The philosophy is true because the book works on an audience
The book can be skilled while the philosophy is false
The philosophy can be true while the book is clumsy
What the work does is a different question from whether you agree

feedback.note: Truth because it works on an audience is the pragmatic substitution of effect for fact. The other lines keep the split: skill without truth, truth without skill, and the esthetic question distinguished from agreement. Audience effect does not certify a metaphysics, and it is not itself the esthetic judgment of what the work does.

exercises.prompt: Which error says the value is simply in the object, so no one needs a method of judgment?

choices.text: The worth is revealed in the work, so judging what it does is unnecessary
You judge by the selective re-creation the work presents
Skill is identified by looking at how the means are controlled
A false view can still be embodied with great control

feedback.note: Intrinsic worth, revealed with no method, skips the question of what the work does. The method is to look at the selective re-creation and at the control of its means. A false view can be skillfully embodied, which an intrinsic stamp of value would not explain, because the stamp would have to be either simply there or simply absent. Judgment is a method, not a revelation.

exercises.prompt: Build the independence of the verdicts in the order that keeps its meaning.

tokens.text: , so neither verdict substitutes for the other

feedback.note: Skill and truth can come apart in either direction, so neither verdict substitutes for the other. One vote, cast by a crowd's reaction, collapses them into a pragmatic effect. The substitutes change the claim because a skilled false view and a clumsy true view are both possible. Agreement is not skill, and skill is not a proof.

exercises.prompt: When does a theme belong inside an esthetic judgment?

choices.text: When the work's own means carry the abstract meaning
When a lecture beside the work states a true sentence
When the reader already agrees with the sentence
When the theme is printed on a card and the work is blank

feedback.note: A theme enters the esthetic judgment when the means carry it, because the judgment asks what the work shows. A true lecture, prior agreement, and a card beside a blank work are outside the re-creation. They can be philosophically interesting and still not be what the work does. Carrying is the test.

exercises.prompt: The dialogue is one long speech of the author's thesis, and the events never make it concrete. What is the esthetic fault?

choices.text: The means do not carry the meaning; a lecture stands in for the re-creation
The fault is that speeches use words
The fault is that a theme is an abstract meaning
There is no fault, because teaching is the purpose of art

feedback.note: A speech that replaces events teaches the thesis instead of showing it. Words are not the fault, and an abstract meaning is exactly what a theme is when the means carry it. Teaching is not the purpose. The fault is the substitution of a lecture for the selective re-creation, so the theme is announced and not embodied. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: A story never states its thesis, yet every selected event shows that a choice has consequences. Where is the theme?

choices.text: Carried by the concretes of the story
Missing, because a theme exists only as a slogan in a preface
Missing, because abstract meaning is not allowed in art
Located only in an interview the author gave later

feedback.note: The events show the meaning, so the theme is carried whether or not a sentence states it. A preface slogan is not required. Abstract meaning is allowed; it is what the concretes carry. An interview is outside the work. The esthetic fact is the embodiment, not the presence of a label. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the judgment it supports.

pairs.right: The means carry the meaning
A lecture stands in for the art

pairs.left: A true sentence in the preface only
pairs.right: A philosophical claim the work has not shown
The concretes that do the showing

feedback.note: Embodiment is carrying. A speech in place of events is a lecture. A preface sentence, however true, has not been shown. The judgment weighs the concretes. Confusing a true sentence with a carried theme treats teaching as showing, which contradicts the purpose of art and leaves the means unexamined.

exercises.prompt: Complete the test that admits a theme into the judgment.

parts.text: The theme counts when the work's means

feedback.note: Carry names embodiment by the means. Replaces names the lecture that stands in for the work. Erases would deny meaning altogether, and prices would turn the test into a market fact. The esthetic question is whether the concretes show the meaning. A true lecture that replaces them has not passed that test. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: Which standard repeats the purpose of art inside this judgment?

choices.text: The work should show the meaning, not teach it in place of the re-creation
The work should teach the meaning and treat the scenes as optional
The work should hide every meaning so judgment has nothing to see
The work should match your philosophy before its means matter

feedback.note: Showing the meaning is the purpose; teaching it while the scenes are optional inverts the purpose. Hiding every meaning leaves no re-creation to judge. Matching your philosophy first collapses esthetic judgment into agreement. The standard is the means: do they carry the theme, or does a lecture do a job the work does not do?

exercises.prompt: A true theme is badly carried, and a false theme is brilliantly carried. What does carrying decide?

choices.text: The esthetic question of what the work does, not which theme is philosophically true
That the true theme is the better art, however badly it is carried
That the false theme is philosophically true, because the carrying is brilliant
Nothing, because carrying refers only to the printer

feedback.note: Carrying decides what the work does as art. It does not make a badly shown truth into a success, and it does not make a brilliantly shown falsehood philosophically true. Those two inferences collapse skill and truth. Carrying is embodiment by the means, not a printer's errand. The same split applies in both directions.

exercises.prompt: Build the test for a theme in the order that keeps its meaning.

tokens.text: , not by a lecture beside it

feedback.note: The theme must be carried by the work's own means, not by a lecture beside it. A true slogan pasted on afterward can be philosophically right and esthetically idle. The substitutes change the test, because the judgment asks what the selective re-creation shows. A sentence outside the concretes has not been shown.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the esthetic standard when you oppose the work's philosophy?

choices.text: The standard stays the same: what the work does as a selective re-creation
The standard is suspended, and opposition is the whole verdict
The standard becomes a hunt for faults that agreement would excuse
The standard becomes agreement, which you then withhold

feedback.note: Opposition does not change the standard. The question remains what the work does as a selective re-creation. Suspending the standard, hunting faults you would excuse in an ally, or withholding agreement and calling that the esthetic verdict are one collapse. You may reject the philosophy and still judge the re-creation by the same method.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the standard when you welcome the philosophy?

choices.text: The standard stays the same, and welcome is not a gift of esthetic success
The standard is relaxed, because allies need not show their theme
The standard is replaced by gratitude
The standard now asks only whether you agree

feedback.note: Welcome is philosophical agreement, not an esthetic gift. Relaxing the standard for allies, replacing it with gratitude, or asking only whether you agree are the same collapse from the friendly side. The work you welcome still has to show its view by its means. Loyalty does not carry a theme the concretes do not carry.

exercises.prompt: Two novels embody the view that man can choose. One plots a real alternative. The other states the line and wanders. You hold the view. How do you judge?

choices.text: By the same standard: the first carries the view, and the second does not
Both succeed, because you welcome the view
Both fail, because a view you hold cannot be judged
The second succeeds more, because it teaches the line outright

feedback.note: The shared philosophy does not equalize the works. The plotted alternative shows volition; the wandering statement teaches a line and does not carry it. Welcome cannot pass both, and holding the view does not make judgment impossible. Teaching the line outright is the purpose art does not have. One standard sorts them.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the move the standard requires.

pairs.right: Judge the re-creation by the same standard
Do not grant success as a reward for agreement
What the work does as a selective re-creation
Agreement or opposition used as the esthetic verdict

feedback.note: Opposition and welcome are answered by the same question: what the work does as a selective re-creation. Using agreement or opposition as the verdict collapses that question into loyalty. The standard does not loosen for allies or tighten into a hunt against opponents. Skill and truth remain able to come apart in both camps.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule that covers both attitudes.

parts.text: for a work you oppose and for a work you

feedback.note: Standard names the esthetic test, and welcome names the friendly case that must take the same test as opposition. A slogan and a price are not that test. The rule forbids a double method: harshness for the philosophy you reject and a gift of success for the philosophy you accept. Both works are judged by what they show. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: Someone says enemies are judged only by whether their ideas are evil, and friends only by loyalty. What is the error?

choices.text: It drops one standard for two loyalties, which is subjectivism about judgment
It keeps what the work does at the center of both cases
It separates philosophical agreement from esthetic judgment
It allows skill and truth to come apart

feedback.note: Two loyalties are two standards, and they make the verdict depend on whose side you are on. That is subjectivism about judgment. The right method keeps what the work does at the center, separates agreement from the esthetic question, and allows skill and truth to come apart. The remark does none of those things. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: You oppose a deterministic novel and welcome a volitional one. The deterministic novel is the more rigorous re-creation. What must you be able to say?

choices.text: The philosophy you oppose is embodied with greater skill than the one you welcome
The welcomed view is automatically the better art
The opposed view cannot be skillfully embodied
Skill on the opposed side must be renamed clumsiness

feedback.note: One standard requires you to grant the greater skill where the re-creation is more rigorous, even though you reject the philosophy. Automatic victory for the welcomed view, a ban on skill in the opposed view, and renaming skill as clumsiness are loyalty tests. They refuse the split between what the work does and whether its view is true. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule of application in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Apply the same esthetic standard to works you welcome and to works you oppose. A loyalty test that changes with agreement is the collapse. The substitutes change the rule, because the question is what each work does as a selective re-creation. Welcome and opposition answer a different question and must not grade the art.

exercises.prompt: Where does Romanticism sit, and what names it?

choices.text: It is a school of art inside esthetics, named by its view of man
It is a further branch beside metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and politics
It is a mood, named by how much feeling a work displays
It is a political program, named by a campaign

feedback.note: Romanticism is a category of art, so it sits inside esthetics, and a school is named by its view of man. It is not an extra branch of philosophy beside the study of art. Amount of feeling names an emotion-oriented mood, which is the popular substitute. A campaign would place it in politics, which drops the esthetic classification. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: Why is "it feels more" not a way to locate this school?

choices.text: A school is classified by its premise about man, not by an emotion-oriented mood
Feeling is the premise that defines every school in the same way
Esthetics studies moods, and views of man belong only to politics
Romanticism sits outside art, in a treatise with no works

feedback.note: Feeling more treats Romanticism as an emotion-oriented mood. The school is located by the view of man it embodies. Feeling is not the shared premise of every school. Esthetics studies art, not moods as such, and a view of man in art is not thereby a political program. The school is a category of art, so it does not sit outside works.

exercises.prompt: A reader calls a novel Romantic because the scenes are exciting, and never asks what it presents man as being. What has been dropped?

choices.text: The classification by a view of man, replaced by a thrill
The placement of the school inside esthetics, which the thrill preserves
Nothing, because excitement is the definition of the school
The possibility that a work of art can have a premise

feedback.note: Excitement is an emotion-oriented test. The school is named by its view of man, so the reader dropped the classifying premise. A thrill does not preserve the esthetic placement in any serious way, because it never reaches the premise. Excitement is not the definition. Works of art can embody a premise; that is how a school is identified.

exercises.prompt: Match each name to the place it has in this classification.

pairs.right: The study of art, inside which schools are placed
A category named by its fundamental view of man
The popular substitute that does not name a school

feedback.note: Esthetics is the study, a school is a category inside it named by a view of man, and an emotion-oriented mood is the substitute that fails to classify. Romanticism is the volition-oriented school, not a fifth branch and not a feeling. Confusing the mood with the school leaves the view of man out of the classification.

exercises.prompt: Complete the statement that places Romanticism inside esthetics.

parts.text: of art, named by its view of

feedback.note: School names the kind of category, and man names what the category is about. Mood would make it emotion-oriented, and price would make it a market fact. Neither locates Romanticism inside esthetics. The view that names this particular school is the recognition of volition, which the placement prepares and does not replace with a feeling.

exercises.prompt: Which classification commits the subjectivist error about schools of art?

choices.text: Naming the school by whether the work feels exciting to you
Naming the school by the view of man it embodies
Placing the school inside the study of art
Refusing to treat the school as a branch of politics

feedback.note: Excitement-to-you makes the classification depend on a personal feeling, which is subjectivism. The school is named by the view of man in the work, placed inside esthetics, and it is not a branch of politics. Those three moves keep a public premise rather than a private thrill. The error is the appeal to how the work feels to the classifier. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: A historian says Romanticism is whatever artists of one century felt, so the view of man is irrelevant. What is the mistake?

choices.text: A period mood replaces classification by a view of man
A school may not be discussed in historical order at all
Esthetics forbids any mention of when a work was made
A view of man cannot be embodied in a work of art

feedback.note: A century's fashion is not the fundamental characteristic of the school. History can be told after the school is defined by its view of man; the mistake is making the period replace that view. Dates are not forbidden. The view of man is exactly what a school of art embodies. The historian's "so" drops the premise that does the classifying. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: Build the placement of the school in the order that keeps its meaning.

tokens.text: named by its view of man

feedback.note: Romanticism is a school inside esthetics named by its view of man. An emotion-oriented mood and a branch of politics are the two misplacements. Either substitute changes the claim, because the category is artistic and the naming premise is about man, not about how much feeling the style seems to contain and not about a campaign.

exercises.prompt: What principle defines Romanticism as a category of art?

choices.text: Man possesses the faculty of volition
Man is determined by forces he cannot choose
Man knows by feeling rather than by reason
Man must escape facts in order to be free

feedback.note: Romanticism is based on the recognition that man possesses volition. Determinism is the premise it rejects. Knowing by feeling is mysticism, and escape from facts is a refusal of reality. Neither is the faculty of volition. The defining principle is that man can choose, not that he feels more or flees the facts. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: A novel's climax follows from a choice the hero could have refused. Which premise makes that structure Romantic?

choices.text: The recognition that man possesses volition
The premise that the hero's act was fixed before his birth
The premise that the climax is a random shock
The premise that choice is an illusion the style should hide

feedback.note: A climax that follows from a choice that could have been refused embodies volition. An act fixed before birth is determinism. A random shock denies purposeful connection. Hiding choice as an illusion denies the faculty the school recognizes. Only the open alternative makes the structure Romantic.

exercises.prompt: A writer says, "My characters choose, but only because fate put the choice into them." What premise is that?

choices.text: Determinism, which denies the volition Romanticism requires
Volition, because the word choose appears
A grammar correction of the characters' motives
A price set on the outcome

feedback.note: If fate stuffed the act into them, they did not possess the faculty of volition; the word choose is doing no work. That is determinism. Grammar and price are not premises about man. The Romantic premise requires a choice that could have gone another way, not a label pasted on a fated outcome. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the premise it expresses.

pairs.right: The faculty of choice the school recognizes in man
The category of art based on that recognition
The denial of choice, however the wording sounds

feedback.note: Volition is the faculty, Romanticism is the category of art based on recognizing it, and a fated act denies it even if someone calls the act a choice. The match keeps the premise, the school, and the counterfeit apart. Feeling more, or escaping facts, would not fill any of these three places.

exercises.prompt: Complete the premise that defines the school.

feedback.note: Volition is the faculty the school recognizes, and determinism is the denial of it. Mysticism and escape are different errors: one bypasses reason, the other flees facts. They are not the name of the premise. The school is volition-oriented, so the first blank cannot be a mood and the second cannot be a synonym for choice. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish as the basis of Romanticism?
exercises.quote: Romanticism is a category of art based on the recognition of the principle that man possesses the faculty of volition.

choices.text: It is a category of art based on the recognition that man possesses volition
It is a category of art based on the denial that man can choose
It is a mood based on the intensity of emotion
It is an escape from facts, based on mysticism

feedback.quote: Romanticism is a category of art based on the recognition of the principle that man possesses the faculty of volition.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "What Is Romanticism?," The Romantic Manifesto, 99
feedback.note: The passage bases the category on one principle: man possesses volition. Denial of choice is the opposite premise. Intensity of emotion makes it a mood, and escape or mysticism makes it a flight from reality. Those readings fail because the sentence names a faculty of choice, not a feeling and not a rejection of facts.

exercises.prompt: Which error treats volition as something a work may drop and still remain Romantic?

choices.text: The school can keep the label and present men as unable to choose
A Romantic plot depends on a choice that could have gone another way
The premise is about man's faculty, not about a costume
Recognizing volition is what places the work in the school

feedback.note: If men are presented as unable to choose, the defining principle is gone and the label cannot save the work. The other lines state the premise correctly: an open choice, a faculty rather than a costume, and recognition of volition as the placement. The error is thinking the school is a tag that survives the denial of its own principle. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: Build the premise in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Romanticism is based on the recognition that man possesses volition. That man is determined reverses the premise. That feeling replaces facts turns the school into mysticism or an escape. Either substitute changes the claim, because the category of art is defined by the faculty of choice, not by determinism and not by emotion.

exercises.prompt: In this contrast, what view of man does Naturalism present?

choices.text: Men as determined
Men as beings who possess volition
Men as mystics who know by escaping facts
Men as moods, with no nature to present

feedback.note: Naturalism, in this contrast, presents men as determined. Volition is the Romantic premise, not the naturalist one. Mysticism and escape are a different mistake about knowledge, not this contrast. A mood with no nature would not be a view of man at all. The opposed schools divide on whether man can choose. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: How does that school try to present such men?

choices.text: By trying to record them without a value-directed plot
By a purposeful progression of chosen acts toward a climax
By stressing a choice the agent could have refused
By selecting events according to the judgment that man can achieve his values

feedback.note: The naturalist method, in this contrast, tries to record determined men without a value-directed plot. A purposeful progression, an open choice, and selection by man's efficacy are Romantic, because they depend on volition. Recording without that plot is the method that follows from treating men as unable to choose.

exercises.prompt: A novel moves from accident to accident, and the narrator insists the man could not have acted otherwise. Which method is that?

choices.text: The presentation of a determined man, without a value-directed plot
Romanticism, because the man suffers and suffering is feeling
Romanticism, because any sequence of events is already a plot
Neither school, because only a poem can hold a view of man

feedback.note: Accidents plus the insistence that he could not have acted otherwise present a determined man and refuse a value-directed plot. Suffering does not make the work Romantic; that treats the school as feeling more. Any sequence is not a plot. A view of man is not confined to poetry. The method is the naturalist contrast.

exercises.prompt: Match each label to the view or method it names.

pairs.right: Man possesses the faculty of volition
Men are presented as determined
Try to record them without a value-directed plot

feedback.note: The premises contradict each other: volition against determinism. The naturalist method is the attempt to record without a value-directed plot, which follows from that denial of choice. Suffering, period costume, and intensity of feeling do not sort these rows, because none of them is the view of man at issue.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast between Naturalism and a value-directed plot.

A sermon is a moral lecture, not the thing Naturalism omits. The contrast is choice against determinism, and a purposeful plot against a record. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: Why does "he suffered, so the work is Romantic" fail as a classification?

choices.text: It treats Romanticism as feeling more, and misses the contrast with determinism
It correctly uses suffering as the definition of volition
It shows that Naturalism denies the existence of pain
It shows that a plot is any sad event

The classification asks whether man is presented as able to choose or as determined, and whether the work has a value-directed plot or tries to record without one. Naturalism does not deny pain. A sad event is not a plot. The remark fails because it uses feeling as the test.

exercises.prompt: A book explains every act as the neighborhood's product and adds details in the order a camera would catch them. What is the combined mark?

choices.text: Determined men, and an attempt to record without a value-directed plot
Volition, embodied in a chosen climax
A fantasy cut off from any intelligible subject
A metaphysics proved by the number of details

feedback.note: The neighborhood as the producer of every act is determinism, and the camera order is the attempt to record without a value-directed plot. That is the naturalist contrast, not a Romantic climax. The subject may still be intelligible, so it is not a fantasy. A pile of details does not prove a metaphysics. The mark is the premise plus the method.

exercises.prompt: Build the contrast in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Naturalism presents men as determined and tries to record them without a value-directed plot. As volitional beings, and through a chosen climax, are the Romantic side of the contrast. Substituting them would change the claim into its opposite, because the schools divide on whether man can choose and on whether the work is a purposeful progression or a record.

exercises.prompt: How must Romanticism be defined, by the fundamental characteristic?

choices.text: As the volition-oriented school
As an emotion-oriented mood
As mysticism about an unknowable realm
As an escape from facts

feedback.note: By the rule of fundamentality, Romanticism must be defined as the volition-oriented school. An emotion-oriented mood takes a consequence, or a popular impression, for the essence. Mysticism claims a way of knowing that bypasses reason. Escape from facts refuses reality. Neither is the recognition that man possesses volition. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: Why is "feeling more" the wrong definition, even when a Romantic work is deeply moving?

choices.text: Emotion is not the fundamental characteristic; volition is
A Romantic work is required to be emotionally blank
Volition means the absence of any values
A school may be named only by its spelling

feedback.note: A Romantic work may move a reader because it shows volition in action. The emotion is not what defines the school. Requiring emotional blankness denies that consequence. Volition is not the absence of values; values are what a chooser pursues. Spelling is irrelevant. Fundamentality picks the premise about man's faculty, not the feeling it can produce.

exercises.prompt: A painter says, "I am a Romantic because I refuse the facts and paint only what a vision revealed." Which errors are those?

choices.text: Mysticism and escape from facts, not the volition-oriented definition
The recognition that man possesses volition
A value-directed plot about a human choice
A re-creation of an intelligible subject

feedback.note: A vision that reveals, and a refusal of the facts, are mysticism and escape. Romanticism recognizes volition inside reality; it does not bypass reason or flee what exists. A value-directed plot and an intelligible subject would be artistic achievements of a very different kind. The painter's sentence defines a mood of flight, not the school.

exercises.prompt: Match each label to the status it has in the definition.

pairs.right: The fundamental definition of Romanticism
The popular substitute the definition rejects
A claim to knowledge that bypasses reason
A refusal of reality, not a recognition of volition

feedback.note: Only the volition-oriented school is the definition. The emotion-oriented mood is the substitute that feels like a definition and is not. Mysticism and escape are further confusions: one about knowledge, one about reality. A passionate flight from facts can be emotionally intense and still fail to be Romantic, because intensity is not the fundamental trait.

exercises.prompt: Complete the required definition and the substitute it rejects.

feedback.note: Volition-oriented names the fundamental characteristic, and mood names the popular substitute. Mystic and escapist name the further errors of revelation and flight from facts. They do not fill the definition. The school is not feeling more. Emotion may be present in the work because values are at stake, and it still does not define the school.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about how Romanticism must be defined?
exercises.quote: Following the rule of fundamentality, it is as a volition-oriented school that Romanticism must be defined—and it is in terms of this essential characteristic that the nature and history of Romantic literature can be traced and understood.

choices.text: It must be defined as the volition-oriented school, by that essential trait
It must be defined as an emotion-oriented mood
It must be defined as mysticism, by the feeling of escape
It must be defined by the fashions of one historical decade

feedback.quote: Following the rule of fundamentality, it is as a volition-oriented school that Romanticism must be defined—and it is in terms of this essential characteristic that the nature and history of Romantic literature can be traced and understood.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "What Is Romanticism?," The Romantic Manifesto, 106
feedback.note: The passage names volition as the essential characteristic, and says the nature and history of the literature are understood in those terms. An emotion-oriented mood, mysticism, and a decade's fashions are the substitutes fundamentality rejects. History is traced by the premise; the premise is not replaced by the history. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence keeps emotion in its proper place?

choices.text: A work may move the reader deeply because it shows volition, and the emotion does not define the school
If the work moves the reader, it is Romantic, whatever it says about choice
If the work acknowledges choice, any feeling disqualifies it
Escape from facts is Romantic whenever the escape is passionate

feedback.note: Emotion can be a consequence of showing a real choice; it is not the defining trait. Movement alone, regardless of the premise about choice, is the emotion-oriented definition. Banning feeling treats a consequence as a disqualification. Passionate escape is still escape, not volition. The proper place of emotion is downstream of the premise.

exercises.prompt: Build the definitional rule in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Romanticism must be defined as the volition-oriented school, not as an emotion-oriented mood. Mysticism and escape from facts are further false definitions. Any of those substitutes changes the claim, because the essential characteristic is man's faculty of volition. Feeling, revelation, and flight do not become fundamental by being intense.

exercises.prompt: What is a plot, in the sense that belongs to this school?

choices.text: A purposeful progression of logically connected events leading to the resolution of a climax
Any sequence of episodes, including a chain of accidents
The theme stated as a slogan in the preface
A mood sustained for the length of the work

feedback.note: A plot is a purposeful progression of logically connected events leading to the resolution of a climax. A chain of accidents lacks the purpose. A preface slogan is not the progression, and a sustained mood is the emotion-oriented substitute. The definition requires purpose, logical connection, and a resolved climax, which determinism does not supply.

exercises.prompt: Why does the volitional premise make a plot of that kind possible?

choices.text: Purpose and a climax that resolves chosen action depend on men who can choose
A plot is possible only if men are determined, so events cannot branch
A plot replaces reality with an escape, so volition is irrelevant
A plot is a feeling, so the premise about man never enters it

feedback.note: Purpose means an end an agent can adopt, and the climax resolves events connected to that end. If men are determined, the progression is not chosen. Escape would cut the plot off from reality, which a re-creation does not do. A feeling is not a plot. Volition is what makes the purposeful structure intelligible.

exercises.prompt: Events are logically connected, the hero chooses a purpose, and the climax resolves it. Why does this belong in esthetics as Romantic art?

choices.text: The work shows volition in a plot, a selective re-creation of a view of man
The work proves volition by a formal deduction printed as dialogue
The work escapes facts by making the choice unreal
The work is Romantic only because the climax produces a strong feeling

feedback.note: The plot shows the metaphysical appraisal that man can choose, which is what places the school in esthetics: art concretizes that view. Dialogue that tries to prove the premise treats art as a lecture. An unreal choice would be an escape from facts. Strong feeling at the climax does not define the school. The belonging is the shown volition.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the place it has in this account.

pairs.right: The premise that makes purposeful action intelligible
Logically connected events resolved in a climax
Events presented without that value-directed progression
The view of man shown in the work, not proved in a lecture

feedback.note: Volition is the premise, the plot is the purposeful progression it makes possible, the naturalist record is the contrast, and the esthetic place is the showing of that view. Art's purpose is to show, not to teach a proof. A string of accidents is not a plot, and a strong feeling is not the reason the school belongs in esthetics. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition of a plot as a purposeful progression.

feedback.note: Purposeful names the direction, and climax names the resolution. Accidental would describe the chain of events the definition excludes. Mood would turn the plot back into an emotion-oriented substitute. A plot also requires logical connection among the events. Without purpose and a resolving climax, the sequence is a record, not this structure. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about a plot?
exercises.quote: A plot is a purposeful progression of logically connected events leading to the resolution of a climax.

choices.text: A plot is a purposeful, logically connected progression resolved in a climax
A plot is a chain of accidents with no purpose connecting them
A plot is an emotion-oriented mood, not a progression of events
A plot is a record of determined men with no chosen climax

feedback.quote: A plot is a purposeful progression of logically connected events leading to the resolution of a climax.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "What Is Romanticism?," The Romantic Manifesto, 100
feedback.note: The passage requires purpose, logical connection, and the resolution of a climax. A chain of accidents drops the purpose. A mood drops the progression of events. A record of determined men drops the choice a climax of this kind resolves. Those are the naturalist or emotion-oriented substitutes, and the sentence admits none of them. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: A manuscript is a string of disasters explained entirely by heredity, with no purpose the characters could have adopted. Why does it lack a plot in this sense?

choices.text: It has no purposeful progression toward the resolution of a chosen climax
It lacks a plot because it mentions human beings
It lacks a plot because the sentences are grammatical
It has a plot, because disasters in a row are a purpose

feedback.note: Heredity as the whole explanation is determinism, and disasters in a row are not a purpose the characters adopted. Mentioning human beings is not the defect, and grammar is not a plot. Calling the row a purpose confuses a sequence with a purposeful progression. What is missing is the volitional structure the definition names.

exercises.prompt: Build the definition of a plot in the order that keeps its meaning.

tokens.text: leading to the resolution of a climax

feedback.note: A plot is a purposeful progression of logically connected events leading to the resolution of a climax. A chain of accidents and an emotion-oriented mood drop purpose or drop events. Either substitute changes the claim. The structure belongs in esthetics because it shows volition; it does not prove a doctrine, and it is not a feeling sustained in place of action.

exercises.prompt: Which statement gives the definition of art?

choices.text: A selective re-creation of reality according to metaphysical value-judgments
An unselective record of everything in front of the artist
A fantasy cut off from reality, with no intelligible subject
A useful object, identified by the job it can perform

feedback.note: Art is a selective re-creation of reality according to metaphysical value-judgments. An unselective record drops selection, and a fantasy cut off from reality drops the re-creation. Usefulness mistakes a practical fact for the definition, because a tool is not yet that re-creation.

exercises.prompt: A novelist keeps the events that embody man as able to choose, and leaves the rest out. Which clause of the definition is he using?

choices.text: Selection according to a metaphysical value-judgment
A duty to record every event at equal weight
A turn away from reality into a private world
A calculation of what the book will cost to print

feedback.note: Keeping some events and dropping others, because they embody a view of man, is selection according to a metaphysical value-judgment. Equal recording abandons selection. A private world abandons reality. Price mistakes the standard of selection for a cost, so it does not name the clause he is using.

exercises.prompt: A portrait stresses a resolute face, omits a cluttered room, and does so because the painter holds that a person can choose. Why does this meet the definition?

choices.text: It selectively re-creates a real subject by a metaphysical appraisal
It meets the definition only if the sitter agrees
It meets the definition because the paint was costly
It meets the definition because nothing was omitted

feedback.note: The portrait is a selective re-creation of a recognizable person, guided by the appraisal that a person can choose. Agreement is a separate question, and cost is not a metaphysical value-judgment. The claim that nothing was omitted denies the selection the work actually performs, so it misstates why the portrait qualifies.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of the definition to the work it does.

pairs.right: The artist includes, omits, and stresses
The work presents an intelligible subject drawn from reality
Fundamental appraisals of man and existence guide the choice

feedback.note: The definition needs all three parts because each does a different job. Selection names the including, omitting, and stressing. Re-creation names an intelligible subject drawn from reality, not a fantasy. Metaphysical value-judgments are the standard of that choice, not a price and not a grammar tip.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition with the two terms that name its method and its standard.

parts.text: re-creation of reality according to metaphysical

feedback.note: Selective names the artist's choice of what to include, omit, and stress. Value-judgments names the metaphysical standard of that choice. Unselective would cancel the choice, and prices would replace an appraisal of man and existence with a cost. Either substitute destroys the definition. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the nature of art?

Art records everything and adds no appraisal of man or existence
Art is a fantasy whose subject need not be intelligible

feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Art and Cognition," The Romantic Manifesto, 45
feedback.note: The passage states the definition: selection, a re-creation of reality, and the artist's metaphysical value-judgments. An unselective record drops the first part, a fantasy drops the tie to reality, and a price treats the standard as a market fact. Those readings contradict the sentence because it names all three parts.

exercises.prompt: Someone says the metaphysical value-judgments in the definition are a sale price and a grammar tip. What is the mistake?

choices.text: They are fundamental appraisals of man and existence, not a price or a grammar tip

The definition really does mean a rule of grammar
The definition names no standard of selection at all

feedback.note: A metaphysical value-judgment appraises man and existence: whether the universe is knowable, whether man can choose, whether he can achieve his values. Calling it a price or a grammar tip replaces that appraisal with a cost or a usage rule. The definition does not leave the standard unnamed, because the according-to clause states it.

exercises.prompt: Build the definition in the order that keeps its meaning.

tokens.text: a fantasy cut off from reality

feedback.note: The claim runs from art, to selective re-creation, to reality, to the metaphysical standard. An unselective record drops the choice, and a fantasy cut off from reality drops the subject. Either substitute changes the definition, because art is neither a dump of facts nor a world with no intelligible tie to what exists.

exercises.prompt: What does selective mean in the definition of art?

choices.text: The artist includes, omits, and stresses aspects of reality
The artist records every aspect at equal emphasis
The artist includes only what no one can recognize
The artist copies a scene and then refuses to emphasize anything

feedback.note: Selective means the artist includes, omits, and stresses. Equal recording is the unselective record the definition rejects. A subject no one can recognize ceases to be a re-creation of reality. Refusing emphasis drops stress, which is one of the three acts of selection, so it is not a fuller fidelity. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: Why is an unselective record not yet the re-creation art names?

choices.text: It includes without omitting or stressing, so no judgment directs it
It fails only when the printing is uneven
It fails because reality cannot be referred to at all
It fails because any stress is a lie about the facts

feedback.note: An unselective record keeps everything at one weight, so it does not include, omit, and stress according to a judgment. Uneven printing is a production fault, not this distinction. Reality remains the thing re-created. Stress is emphasis, not a lie, and treating it as a lie confuses selection with fraud.

exercises.prompt: A novelist cuts three subplots and stresses one choice that commits the hero. What is that, as selection?

choices.text: Omission of some events and stress on the one that matters
A failure, because a re-creation must keep every subplot
Fantasy, because any omission cuts the work off from reality
A grammar rule about how short a chapter may be

feedback.note: Cutting subplots and stressing one choice is omission and stress, which is what selective means. Keeping every subplot would be an unselective record. Omission does not by itself create a fantasy, because the stressed choice is still a human action drawn from reality. A length rule mistakes selection for grammar.

exercises.prompt: Match each act of selection to what the artist is doing.

pairs.right: Keep the aspects the judgment treats as essential
Leave out aspects that do not serve that judgment
Give greater weight to what the judgment ranks as fundamental

feedback.note: Include, omit, and stress are three acts of one selection, because each is directed by the same judgment. Omitting is not erasing reality, and stressing is not adding a private world. An account that keeps only one act, or that treats them as a grammar exercise, leaves out what selective means.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two acts so that selection keeps what is essential.

feedback.note: Selection includes what the judgment ranks as essential and omits the rest. Reversing the verbs would drop the essential and keep the irrelevant, which is not selection. Invents would turn the work into a fantasy cut off from reality. Prices would make cost the standard. Neither substitute works, because selection acts on aspects of reality by a metaphysical judgment.

exercises.prompt: A painter stresses a cracked wall and omits a garden because the work holds that effort ends in ruin. Is that still selection?

No. Selection may stress only victories
No. Omission is allowed only when the omitted thing is ugly
No. Stress counts only when a crowd prefers it

feedback.note: Selection includes, omits, and stresses according to the artist's metaphysical appraisal, and a bleak appraisal is still an appraisal. Limiting stress to victories, or omission to ugliness, substitutes a cheerfulness rule. A crowd's preference substitutes subjectivism. The cracked wall is selected because of the judgment, not in spite of it.

exercises.prompt: Which remark confuses selection with cutting the work off from reality?

choices.text: If the artist omits anything, the work is no longer about reality
Omission can keep the aspects the artist judges fundamental
Stress directs attention and does not replace the subject

feedback.note: Omission is part of selection, and the work remains a re-creation of reality when the subject stays intelligible. The remark treats every omission as a fantasy cut off from reality, which confuses two different errors. The other lines keep inclusion, omission, and stress tied to a subject, so they do not make that mistake.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim about selection in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Selective means the artist includes, omits, and stresses aspects of reality. Recording everything equally is the unselective record, and inventing a private world is a fantasy. Both substitutes drop the definition, because selection is a directed treatment of reality, not a refusal to choose and not a break with the subject.

exercises.prompt: What is a re-creation, as against the two things it is not?

choices.text: An intelligible presentation of reality, not a dump and not a fantasy
A complete inventory of a place, with nothing omitted
A private world the viewer is not meant to recognize
A copy that becomes art by the addition of a caption

feedback.note: A re-creation presents reality again in a form one can grasp. A complete inventory is an unselective record, and an unrecognizable world is a fantasy cut off from reality. A caption does not supply the subject the work itself must present. The definition requires the intelligible re-creation, not those substitutes.

exercises.prompt: A sculptor simplifies a standing man, and a viewer can still see that the subject is a man. What is the status of that stylization?

choices.text: It stays within art, because stylization is limited by intelligibility
It ceases to be art, because any departure from a body-cast is fantasy
It is an unselective record, because simplification keeps more detail
It is art only if no one can tell what the figure is

feedback.note: Stylization is permitted, and its limit is intelligibility: the figure must still be graspable as a man. Forbidding every departure from a cast confuses a re-creation with an unselective cast. Simplification omits detail; it does not record more. Erasing the subject would make the work cease to be art, which is the opposite error.

exercises.prompt: A canvas presents no intelligible subject. What follows for its status as art?

choices.text: It ceases to be art, because a re-creation must present a graspable subject
It is a higher art, because absence of a subject is pure creation
It is an unselective record of everything the eye might see
It remains art, because the maker's feeling needs no subject

feedback.note: If a work presents no intelligible subject, it ceases to be art, because a re-creation of reality has to be representational within the limit of intelligibility. Calling the blank a higher creation treats fantasy as art. An empty subject is not a record of everything. Feeling as a substitute for a subject is subjectivism, and it does not restore the work.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of presentation to the status it has.

pairs.right: Everything included, with nothing stressed by a judgment
No intelligible subject drawn from reality
Reality presented again in a form a viewer can grasp

feedback.note: The three presentations are not degrees of one thing. An unselective record fails by refusing selection, a fantasy fails by leaving reality, and a re-creation keeps an intelligible subject. Mixing them treats a dump, or a world no one can identify, as if it still met the definition of art.

exercises.prompt: Someone says art cannot re-create reality, because the mind never reaches things as they are. What error is that?

choices.text: It denies that a work can present an intelligible subject drawn from reality
It restates the limit that stylization must remain intelligible
It separates an unselective record from a re-creation

feedback.note: The claim that the mind's forms cut us off from things as they are denies the re-creation of reality. Art, on this account, presents an intelligible subject drawn from reality, within the limit of stylization. The remark is not that limit, and it does not distinguish a record from a re-creation. It abandons the subject the definition requires.

Either substitute leaves the definition, because the work is neither a dump of everything present nor a fantasy no one can identify.

The sale price the artist hopes to get
A tip about grammar in the caption
A head count of the figures on the canvas

feedback.note: A metaphysical value-judgment is a fundamental appraisal of man and existence, such as whether the universe is knowable, whether man can choose, and whether he can achieve his values. Price and grammar are the two substitutions this account rejects. A head count is a tally, not an appraisal, so it does not guide selection.

exercises.prompt: Which questions are the metaphysical appraisals that can guide an artist's selection?

choices.text: Is the universe knowable, can man choose, and can he achieve his values?
What will the frame cost, and how should the caption be punctuated?
Which slogan should be printed beside an unrelated picture?
How many tickets were sold on opening night?

feedback.note: The guiding questions appraise existence and man: knowability, volition, and efficacy. Cost and punctuation are a price and a grammar tip. A slogan beside an unrelated picture is not the standard inside the work. Ticket sales are a market result. Those substitutes do not tell the artist what to include, omit, or stress. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: A dramatist selects so that thought succeeds and a choice changes the outcome. Which appraisal is guiding that selection?

choices.text: That man can know, can choose, and can achieve a value by that choice
That man is a puppet of forces he cannot know or resist
That the ticket price should be high
That the dialogue should avoid commas

feedback.note: Thought that succeeds, and a choice that changes the outcome, embody the appraisal that man can know, choose, and achieve. The puppet view is a contrary metaphysical appraisal and would select a different action. Price and comma rules are not appraisals of man and existence, so they do not explain this selection. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: Match each metaphysical question to the appraisal it is.

pairs.right: An appraisal of existence as open to the mind
An appraisal of man as possessing volition
An appraisal of man's efficacy in existence

feedback.note: These three questions are metaphysical value-judgments, not ethical slogans pasted on afterward. Knowability appraises existence, volition appraises man, and efficacy appraises whether he can achieve his values in the world. Treating any of them as a price or a grammar tip leaves out the standard of selection.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two metaphysical questions these judgments ask.

feedback.note: Man is the being who can choose, and existence is what may be knowable. Price and grammar are a cost and a usage tip, not these questions. Putting existence first would ask whether existence can choose, which is not the appraisal. The judgments are fundamental, and the alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

exercises.prompt: What do metaphysical value-judgments do in the making of the work?

choices.text: They set the standard for what the artist includes, omits, and stresses
They replace the subject, so the work need not re-create reality
They are added later, as a price tag
They are a grammar check performed by an editor

feedback.note: The judgments are the standard of selection: they direct inclusion, omission, and stress. They do not cancel the subject, because the work remains a re-creation of reality. A later price tag and an editor's grammar check are the two familiar substitutions, and neither tells the artist which aspects of reality are fundamental.

exercises.prompt: An artist says the only standard is that viewers should feel guilty and donate. What has replaced a metaphysical value-judgment?

choices.text: A moral demand, offered as the purpose, in place of an appraisal of man and existence
The question of whether man can choose
The question of whether the universe is knowable
The question of whether man can achieve his values

feedback.note: Guilt and a demand to donate are a moral campaign, not a fundamental appraisal of man and existence. Moral values can enter later as a consequence of a metaphysical view, but they are not the primary standard of selection. The three metaphysical questions remain the standard this remark has replaced. That reading fails because it answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim about the standard of selection in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Metaphysical value-judgments appraise man and existence and thereby guide selection. A sale price and a grammar correction are the two errors that mimic a standard without appraising anything fundamental. Using either one changes the claim, because the artist would then be choosing by cost or by usage, not by a view of man and existence.

exercises.prompt: Which description keeps selection, a re-creation of reality, and metaphysical value-judgments together?

choices.text: A play shows a human choice, omits the trivial hours, and stresses the choice because man possesses volition
A play records every hour of a day at equal weight and with no appraisal
A play invents an unrecognizable realm and puts the moral in the program
A play is cast by auction, and the highest price decides the meaning

feedback.note: The first play selects, presents an intelligible human action, and uses the appraisal that man possesses volition. The day-long record drops selection. The unrecognizable realm drops reality and pastes a moral beside it. The auction treats a price as the standard. Only the first holds the three parts together.

exercises.prompt: A story is intelligible, but the events are chosen to shock a crowd this week, with no appraisal of man or existence. What is missing?

choices.text: Metaphysical value-judgments as the standard of selection
An alphabet in which the book can be printed
An unselective inventory of a street
A subject no reader can identify

feedback.note: Shock chosen for a crowd is subjectivism, or a pragmatic bid for effect, not a metaphysical value-judgment. The story can be intelligible and still lack the standard of selection. An alphabet is not that standard. An inventory and an unidentifiable subject fail other parts of the definition, which this case has not failed. The rival fails because it changes the principle.

exercises.prompt: A poster says only "Obey and sacrifice," and the figures are interchangeable. Why is this not the art the definition names?

choices.text: It is a propaganda command, not a selective re-creation that shows a view of man and existence
It fails only because paper cannot carry ink
It succeeds because a command is the basic purpose of art
It succeeds because moral pressure replaces the need for a subject

feedback.note: The poster teaches an order instead of showing an intelligible view of man and existence. That is a propaganda poster, and the basic purpose of art is not to teach but to show. Ink is irrelevant. A command is not the purpose, and moral pressure does not replace a subject. The figures carry no metaphysical selection.

exercises.prompt: Match each failed work to the part of the definition it drops.

pairs.right: Drops selection, and becomes an unselective record

pairs.right: Replaces showing with a propaganda command

feedback.note: Each failure drops a different part of one claim. The photograph aims at an unselective record. The fantasy has no intelligible subject. Price, grammar, or a slogan is not a metaphysical appraisal. The poster is propaganda, whose purpose is to teach an order rather than to show a view of man and existence. The substitute fails because it drops the distinction.

exercises.prompt: Complete the place of moral values inside the work.

feedback.note: Moral values follow from the metaphysical appraisal; they are not the primary purpose. Making them the purpose turns the work into a morality play. The alternative fails because it does not state this claim.

Those readings fail because concretization shows the view in the work; it does not discard it, prove it, or sell it.

exercises.prompt: Which work is a news photograph of the kind the definition excludes, and why?

choices.text: One that tries to record every bystander at equal weight, with no metaphysical selection
One that omits a crowd in order to stress a single human choice
One that remains intelligible while simplifying a face
One whose selection is guided by the appraisal that man can choose

feedback.note: The excluded news photograph is the unselective record: everything at equal weight, with no metaphysical value-judgment directing it. Omitting, stressing a choice, simplifying within intelligibility, and selecting by the appraisal that man can choose are acts of a re-creation. They do not become a news record merely because an image is involved.

exercises.prompt: Build the full claim in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: The full claim joins the selective re-creation, the metaphysical standard, and the purpose of showing rather than teaching. A morality play makes moral instruction the purpose. A news photograph of the excluded kind is an unselective record. Either substitute breaks the claim, because moral values are a consequence of the view, not a sermon, and a dump is not a re-creation.

exercises.prompt: What does the phrase a sense of life name?

choices.text: A pre-conceptual, emotional appraisal of man and of existence
An explicit philosophy, stated in definitions and proofs
A tool that discovers facts by means of feeling
A passing reaction to one inconvenience

feedback.note: A sense of life is a pre-conceptual equivalent of metaphysics: an emotional, subconsciously integrated appraisal of man and of existence. An explicit philosophy is the later translation, not the appraisal itself. Feeling does not discover facts, so it is not a tool of cognition. A passing reaction has no such object.

exercises.prompt: Why is a sense of life not a proof of the facts it appraises?

choices.text: It is an emotional appraisal below the level of argument, not evidence
It fails to be a proof only because words are longer than feelings
It becomes a proof whenever the feeling is intense
It proves what man is, but it cannot concern existence

feedback.note: The appraisal is emotional and pre-conceptual, so it is not an argument and not evidence. Length of wording is irrelevant. Intensity does not turn a feeling into a proof; that confuses an appraisal with a tool of cognition. The appraisal concerns both man and existence, so cutting off existence also misstates it.

exercises.prompt: A person says, "I feel the plan will fail, so the feeling has discovered the failure." What error is that?

choices.text: Treating a feeling as a tool that discovers facts
Treating a sense of life as an appraisal of man
Admitting that an appraisal can later be stated in ideas
Naming existence as one object of the appraisal

feedback.note: The feeling expresses an estimate; it does not discover that the plan will fail. Using it as a discovery treats emotion as a tool of cognition. An appraisal of man, a later translation into ideas, and existence as an object are parts of the account, not the error. The error is the claim that the feeling found a fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each name to the thing it actually is.

pairs.right: An emotional, pre-conceptual appraisal of man and existence
Ideas stated and connected at the conceptual level
The error of treating the appraisal as a tool of cognition

feedback.note: A sense of life is the emotional appraisal, an explicit philosophy is the conceptual statement, and feeling used as proof is a confusion of the two. The appraisal can be translated into ideas later, but the feeling does not itself discover facts. Collapsing the three treats a subconscious estimate as if it were already an argument.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about a sense of life?
exercises.quote: A sense of life is a pre-conceptual equivalent of metaphysics, an emotional, subconsciously integrated appraisal of man and of existence.

choices.text: It is a pre-conceptual emotional appraisal of man and of existence
